Based on my search, I can provide you with a comparison between the first satellite ever launched and the latest satellite technology.

## First Satellite: Sputnik 1 (1957)

**Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**, was humanity's first artificial satellite. Its specifications were remarkably simple by today's standards:

| Feature | Specification |
|---------|-------------|
| **Diameter** | 58 cm (23 inches) |
| **Weight** | 83-84 kg |
| **Shape** | Metal sphere with four external antennas |
| **Payload** | Thermometer, fan, radio transmitter, batteries |
| **Orbit** | Elliptical: 230 km (perigee) to 940 km (apogee) |
| **Orbital period** | ~96 minutes |
| **Operational lifespan** | 3 weeks (until batteries died) |
| **Total time in orbit** | Until January 4, 1958 (~3 months) |

Sputnik 1 was extremely basic—essentially a beeping radio transmitter that broadcast temperature data. Its primary significance was political and historical, triggering the Space Race and the formation of NASA.

---

## Latest Satellite Technology (2020s)

Modern satellites have evolved dramatically across multiple categories:

### Communications Satellites
- **Viasat-3** and similar high-capacity satellites provide global broadband internet, including in-flight Wi-Fi
- Support streaming, video conferencing, and online gaming with low latency
- Use advanced Ka-band frequencies with much higher bandwidth

### Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Constellations
- **Starlink** (SpaceX): Over 4,000+ satellites in orbit since 2019
- Orbit at ~2,000 km altitude (vs. Sputnik's 230-940 km)
- Provide global, continuous coverage through coordinated constellations
- Offer lower latency and higher bandwidth than traditional geostationary satellites

### Size and Scale Comparisons

| Satellite | Weight | Comparison to Sputnik 1 |
|-----------|--------|------------------------|
| Sputnik 1 | 84 kg | Baseline |
| Hubble Space Telescope | ~11,110 kg | ~132× heavier |
| Modern geostationary comms satellites | Up to ~7,000 kg | ~83× heavier |
| International Space Station | ~440,000 kg | ~5,000× heavier |

### Technological Advances
| Aspect | Then (1957) | Now (2020s) |
|--------|-------------|-------------|
| **Purpose** | Political/demonstration | Communications, navigation, Earth observation, scientific research, weather monitoring |
| **Lifespan** | 3 weeks | 5-15+ years with solar power |
| **Data transmission** | Simple radio beeps | High-speed broadband, HD video, real-time data |
| **Instruments** | Thermometer, basic radio | Multi-spectral imagers, radar, laser communications, AI-powered systems |
| **Ground stations** | Large directional antennas | Small user terminals, smartphones, integrated devices |
| **Manufacturing** | Custom-built | Standardized small satellites (CubeSats), mass production |
| **Launch costs** | Prohibitively expensive | Reusable rockets dramatically reducing costs |

---

## Key Paradigm Shifts

1. **From single satellites to constellations**: Modern systems use thousands of coordinated satellites rather than lone spacecraft

2. **From massive to miniature**: While some satellites grew enormous, the "New Space" movement has also produced **CubeSats** and small standardized satellites that are even smaller than Sputnik but vastly more capable

3. **From government-only to commercial**: Space is now dominated by private companies (SpaceX, Planet Labs, etc.) rather than solely national space programs

4. **From simple broadcast to two-way interactive services**: Modern satellites enable real-time, bidirectional global communication

The evolution from Sputnik 1's simple 84 kg beeping sphere to today's multi-ton, multi-functional spacecraft—or conversely to swarms of tiny, sophisticated CubeSats—represents perhaps the most dramatic technological transformation of any industry in human history.

Sources:
1. https://astrobiology.nz/sputnik-1-and-the-space-age/
2. https://darwincav.com/sputnik-1-the-first-artificial-satellite/
3. https://www.remotesatellite.com/the-exciting-shift-in-satellite-technology/
4. https://www.spacecapital.com/blogs/satellites-past-present-future
5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/satellite-communication-system
